subject: Biology
title: What Is Coral?
description: A quick win: understand What Is Coral?.

hook.text: Coral looks like rock, feels like stone, but it's actually millions of tiny animals living together.

buildup.text: Each coral polyp is a soft-bodied animal related to jellyfish, with a ring of stinging tentacles.

discovery.text: Polyps secrete calcium carbonate skeletons. Over centuries, these accumulate into massive reef structures.

twist.text: Coral gets its color from symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae that live inside its tissue.

climax.text: The algae provide up to 90% of the coral's energy through photosynthesis—a perfect partnership.

punchline.text: Not a rock. Not a plant. An animal city.

quiz.question: What are coral polyps?
options: Mineral formations on the sea floor

details.summary: Corals are marine invertebrate animals that secrete calcium carbonate skeletons to build reef structures. Most reef-building corals host symbiotic zooxanthellae algae that provide up to 90 percent of the coral's energy through photosynthesis in exchange for shelter and nutrients.
details.whyItMatters: Corals are the architects of the ocean's most biodiverse ecosystems. Understanding coral biology is essential for reef conservation as these animals face existential threats from warming, acidification, and pollution worldwide.
takeaways: Corals are animals, not plants, belonging to the phylum Cnidaria
Zooxanthellae algae provide up to 90 percent of a coral's energy needs
Reef-building corals grow only millimeters to centimeters per year

faq.question: Are corals plants or animals?
faq.answer: Corals are animals, closely related to jellyfish and sea anemones. They are cnidarians with stinging cells for capturing tiny prey. However, reef-building corals host photosynthetic algae inside their tissues, which is why they are often mistaken for plants.

faq.question: How do coral reefs grow?
faq.answer: Individual coral polyps secrete calcium carbonate skeletons beneath their soft tissue. As colonies grow and new polyps bud, the reef structure slowly builds. Growth rates of just millimeters per year mean large reefs take thousands of years to develop.
